teile.einleitung: A kettle is an electric kitchen appliance that brings water to the boil quickly. It has a heater in its base and switches itself off as soon as the water boils. It is useful for tea, instant soups or for heating water in advance for pasta.
wichtigste: A kettle needs electricity to heat.
In many kettles the heater is in the base.
Water usually boils faster in a kettle than in a saucepan on the cooker.
Over time a white layer of limescale forms, which you can remove with vinegar.
You fill it with only as much water as you need, to save electricity.
You must never dip a kettle into the sink and never switch it on empty.

abschnitte.text: A **kettle** is a jug with a built in electric heater. It stands on a base with a cable, from which you can lift it off to pour. On the outside, a scale with marks shows how much water is in it. Most kettles hold between one and two litres.

In the base there is a **heating element**, through which electric current flows and makes it very hot. The heat goes straight into the water, so it gets hot faster than in a saucepan on the cooker. When the water boils, steam rises to a switch with a **bimetallic strip**. This bends in the heat and switches the kettle off automatically.

Tap water contains dissolved **lime**, especially in areas with a lot of limestone, such as the Jura. When the water is heated, the lime settles as a white layer on the bottom. This layer makes the water take longer to boil and uses more electricity. With vinegar or citric acid you can dissolve the limescale and then rinse well.

You fill in only as much water as you really need, because every extra decilitre has to be heated as well. For pasta, you can heat the water in the kettle first and then pour it into the pan. This saves time and often energy too. A descaled kettle also works more economically.

A kettle is an **electrical appliance** and must never be dipped into the sink. Water in the base or on the plug can cause a dangerous electric shock. You never switch it on without water, because it could get too hot; many kettles have **boil dry protection** for this. The cable should not hang over the edge of the table, so that nobody pulls the hot kettle down.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part that turns electric current into heat.
A strip made of two metals that bends when warm and so works as a switch.
A white coating of minerals that were dissolved in the water.
A safety device that switches the appliance off if there is no water in it.

gewusst: A typical kettle has a power of about 2000 watts, much more than a television.
In Great Britain, so many kettles are switched on at the same time during the advert breaks of popular TV programmes that the power stations have to supply more electricity.
The rushing noise just before boiling comes from small steam bubbles collapsing again in the colder water.

teile.einleitung: The washing machine is a household appliance that cleans clothes with water, detergent and movement. In the past, doing the washing was hard manual work that could take a whole day. There is a lot of physics inside a washing machine.
wichtigste: Inside the washing machine a drum with lots of holes turns round.
Water, detergent, heat and movement loosen the dirt from the washing.
At the end the machine spins, turning very fast.
In many Swiss blocks of flats, the washing machine is in the shared laundry room.
Light and dark washing are washed separately, because dark colours can run.
The little pictures on the label show how a garment should be washed.
Before washing, you check the trouser pockets.

abschnitte.text: Inside the machine is a **drum** with many small holes. It fills with water, which a heater warms to the chosen temperature. The drum turns first one way and then the other, so the washing is lifted up and falls back into the water. The **detergent** loosens grease and dirt from the fibres.

At the end the drum turns very fast, often more than 1000 times a minute. The washing is pressed against the drum wall by **centrifugal force**. The water cannot follow and sprays out through the holes. That is why the washing is only damp after the **spin** and dries faster.

In many Swiss blocks of flats, all the families share a **laundry room** in the cellar. A **laundry rota** sets out who may do their washing on which day. There is often a tumble dryer there too, or a drying room with lines. In Switzerland, the rules of the laundry room are sometimes even a topic of conversation between neighbours.

The little pictures on the **care label** show, for example, at how many degrees a garment may be washed. Light and dark washing are kept apart so that no colour runs. A wool jumper can **shrink**, that is, get smaller, if the water is too hot. Before washing, you empty the pockets, because tissues, coins or pens can damage the washing and the machine.

In the past, people washed clothes in a stream or in big tubs and rubbed them on a **washboard**. Then they had to wring them out by hand. Electric washing machines have existed since the beginning of the 20th century. In Swiss households they gradually became common after the Second World War and saved a lot of time.

abschnitte.titel: Washing in an environmentally friendly way
abschnitte.text: The machine uses most of its energy to heat the water. Washing at 30 or 40 degrees instead of 60 degrees saves a lot of electricity. It is worth filling the drum well and not using too much detergent. Modern machines have an **energy label** that shows how economical they are.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rotating container in which the washing lies.
The force that pushes outwards when something spins fast.
A shared room for doing the washing in many Swiss buildings.
A sewn in label with washing instructions shown as little pictures.

gewusst: During the spin, a washing machine drum can turn faster than a car engine when idling.
A sock that disappears sometimes slips between the drum and the rubber seal.
Before there were washing machines, washing day was often the most tiring day of the week.

teile.einleitung: A water pump moves water from one place to another, often upwards too. Without pumps there would be no water from the tap on the top floor, no heating and no cooled car engine. More than 2000 years ago, people already invented clever devices for lifting water.
wichtigste: A water pump moves water.
The old hand pump with a long lever at a well is called a lever pump.
The Archimedes screw lifts water upwards with a turning screw.
A submersible pump is sunk completely in the water.
Most pumps today are driven by an electric motor.
In a car, a water pump pumps cooling water through the engine.
After a storm, pumps pump water out of flooded cellars.

abschnitte.text: A **pump** is a machine that sets liquids in motion. It can push water through pipes or carry it upwards. For this it needs energy, in the past from people, animals or waterwheels, today mostly from an **electric motor**. Pumps are found in washing machines, dishwashers, heating systems and wells. Your heart is a pump too, driving blood round your body.

In a **piston pump**, a piston moves back and forth in a cylinder. When it is pulled back it sucks water in, and when it is pushed forward it presses it out; valves let the water flow in one direction only. In a **centrifugal pump**, an impeller spins very fast and flings the water outwards. Centrifugal pumps are the most common today. A suction pump can suck water up only about 10 metres at most, because the air pressure cannot manage more.

The **Archimedes screw** is a very old invention and is credited to the Greek scientist Archimedes. A sloping screw inside a tube lifts water upwards step by step as it turns. It was used to water fields. Later, **lever pumps** with a long handle were built at village wells. By moving the handle up and down, people brought water up from the depths.

If there is water in the cellar after a storm, the fire brigade pumps it out with pumps. A **submersible pump** is sunk completely in the water for this. In deep wells too, submersible pumps bring up the groundwater. In an aquarium, a small pump moves the water through a filter and adds oxygen to it. The circulation pump of a heating system sends warm water through the radiators.

A car with a petrol engine has a **water pump** that pumps cooling water through the engine. This stops the engine getting too hot. In Switzerland there are also **pumped storage power stations**. They pump water into a higher reservoir when there is plenty of electricity. When electricity is needed, the water flows back down and drives turbines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving cylinder in a pump that sucks water in and pushes it out.
A flap that lets the water flow in one direction only.
A pump that works completely under water.
A power station that pumps water up and so stores energy.

gewusst: At rest, a human heart pumps about five litres of blood a minute.
Today Archimedes screws are also used the other way round as small hydroelectric power stations; they are considered fish friendly.

teile.einleitung: An inflatable beach ball is a popular toy at the swimming pool and by the lake. With it you can watch beautifully how buoyancy works in water. But the German word “Wasserball” also means an exciting team sport played in a swimming pool, which in English is called water polo.
wichtigste: An inflated beach ball floats on top and sinks in only a little way.
It is filled with air and is therefore much lighter than the water it could push aside.
If you push it under water, it is pushed strongly upwards.
If you let go of it under water, it leaps out of the water.
On a lake, the wind easily blows a beach ball away.
A beach ball is not a life saving aid.
Water polo is also a sport in which two teams throw goals in a pool.

abschnitte.text: A **beach ball** for playing with is usually made of thin, colourful plastic. You blow it up with your mouth or with a pump. Almost its whole volume is air, so it is very light. If you let the air out, it goes floppy and can be folded up small. That way it fits in any swimming bag.

Every body in water feels **buoyancy**. It is as big as the weight of the water that the body pushes aside; the Greek **Archimedes** already realised this. A beach ball weighs very little, so it only has to push aside a tiny amount of water to float. That is why it sinks in only a little way. A stone, on the other hand, is heavier than the water it pushes aside and sinks.

If you want to push a big beach ball under water, you need a lot of strength. Under water it pushes aside a great deal of water and is pushed upwards just as strongly. A ball 50 centimetres across displaces about 65 litres, which corresponds to a force like the weight of 65 kilograms. If you let go, it shoots upwards and leaps out of the water. The force of buoyancy turns into movement.

Because a beach ball is so light and sticks up high out of the water, even a gentle **wind** can push it away. On a lake it can quickly be a long way out. You should not swim far out after it, because the ball is not a **life saving aid**. It can roll away or burst and does not carry a person safely. It is better to let the ball go or to get help.

**Water polo** is a team sport played in a swimming pool. Two teams of seven players each, including a goalkeeper, try to throw the ball into the other team's goal. The water is so deep that nobody can stand, so the players have to swim and tread water all the time. Usually you may hold the ball with one hand only. Water polo has been part of the Olympic Games since 1900 and is one of the oldest Olympic team sports.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
A body pushes water aside and takes its place.
A Greek scientist who discovered the law of buoyancy.
A swimming movement that keeps you in one place above the water.

gewusst: During a match, water polo players may not support themselves on the bottom or on the edge of the pool.
A beach ball also floats in the salty sea, where it sinks in even a little less.

teile.einleitung: A water rocket is a home made rocket made from a PET bottle that flies using water and air pressure. It shows in an exciting way how real rockets work. If it is well built, it flies many metres high.
wichtigste: A water rocket is usually made from a PET bottle.
You fill it about one third full with water.
When you pump, high air pressure builds up in the bottle.
At launch the water squirts downwards and the rocket flies upwards.
Cardboard fins make sure it flies straight.
You launch it outdoors in an open field.
At launch you keep your distance, because it shoots off suddenly and fast.

abschnitte.text: A water rocket usually consists of a **PET bottle** standing upside down on a launch pad. It is partly filled with water and pumped up with an air pump. As soon as the stopper opens, the water shoots out and the bottle takes off. With a bicycle pump and some craft materials you can easily build one yourself.

The water rocket works by the **principle of recoil**. When water is pushed downwards with great force, the bottle is pushed upwards with an equally great force. Isaac Newton described this rule as his third **law of motion**: every force has an opposing force. Real rockets work in exactly the same way, except that they push out hot gases instead of water.

When you pump, the air in the bottle is squeezed together, which raises the **air pressure**. The compressed air wants to expand and pushes the water out powerfully. About one third water has proved to be a good filling. With too little water there is hardly any thrust; with too much water there is too little room for the compressed air.

So that the rocket does not wobble, you stick cardboard **fins** onto the bottom. A nose cone made of cardboard or half a bottle makes it more streamlined. A little weight in the nose helps it fly steadily. In schools and competitions, rockets are even fitted with parachutes.

Water rockets are launched only outdoors in an open **field**, far away from roads, windows and people. You pump only up to the pressure the bottle can stand, and you use only undamaged bottles. At launch everyone keeps their distance, because the rocket shoots off suddenly. You never look straight down over the rocket, and you still get wet now and then.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force produced when something is pushed out backwards.
How hard the air presses on a surface.
The stand on which the rocket rests before launch.
A steering surface that keeps the rocket steady in flight.

gewusst: Well built water rockets made of several bottles can fly more than 100 metres high.
After landing, you can simply refill the same rocket and launch it again.
Squid also use the principle of recoil by pushing water out powerfully.

teile.einleitung: Thermal conduction is one of the ways heat travels from a warm place to a cold one. The particles of a substance pass their energy of motion on to their neighbours, without the substance itself flowing. That is why the handle of a metal spoon in hot soup quickly gets warm.
wichtigste: In thermal conduction, energy is passed from particle to particle without any material being carried along.
Heat always flows from the warmer to the colder body.
Metals such as copper are very good conductors of heat.
Materials that conduct heat poorly are called insulators, for example wood, plastic and air.
How much heat flows through a wall depends on the material, thickness, area and temperature difference.
Water conducts heat much better than air.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny particles that are constantly moving. The warmer a substance is, the more strongly its particles jiggle. In **thermal conduction**, fast particles bump into their slower neighbours and so pass on energy. The substance itself stays where it is, unlike in **convection** in water or air.

Metals conduct heat particularly well, because their freely moving electrons carry the energy quickly. **Copper** and silver are among the best conductors of heat, which is why good pans often have a copper base. If a metal spoon stands in hot soup, its handle soon gets warm. A metal railing feels colder in winter than a wooden one, because the metal carries heat away from your hand faster.

Materials that conduct heat poorly are called **insulators**. They include wood, plastic, wool, polystyrene and, above all, still air. That is why wooden spoons and pan handles often have parts made of wood or plastic. Down jackets and wool jumpers keep you warm because they trap a lot of air between their fibres.

How much heat is conducted through a wall each second depends on the material, thickness, area and **temperature difference**. The French mathematician Joseph Fourier described this relationship in the 19th century. Well insulated houses lose less heat in winter and need less energy for heating. In Switzerland there are building standards for this, such as Minergie.

When camping in winter, you put a thick mat under your sleeping bag so that less body heat flows into the cold ground. In water at 15 °C you cool down much faster than in air at 15 °C, because water conducts heat about twenty times better. That is why it is dangerous to swim for a long time in cold lakes or rivers. For the same reason, wet clothes keep you much less warm than dry ones.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that passes heat on quickly, for example copper.
A material that conducts heat only poorly, for example wood or air.
A layer that stops heat escaping from a house.
How much warmer one side is than the other; it drives the flow of heat.

gewusst: Diamond conducts heat even better than copper, which is why a real diamond feels cool.
Under their fur, polar bears have a thick layer of fat that protects them from the cold like an insulator.
A tiled floor and a carpet in the same room are at the same temperature, yet the tiled floor feels much colder.

teile.einleitung: Pond skaters are insects that dart across the surface of ponds and streams on their long, thin legs without sinking. This is made possible by the surface tension of water. They are skilful hunters that catch small animals on the water.
wichtigste: Pond skaters walk on the surface of ponds, lakes and slow streams.
They belong to the true bugs, a group of insects.
Fine, water repellent hairs on their legs stop them from sinking in.
The surface tension of the water carries their low weight.
Pond skaters feed on insects that have fallen into the water.
They detect their prey through the small ripples on the water.
In Switzerland the common pond skater can be seen on many waters.

abschnitte.text: Pond skaters have a narrow, elongated body, which in the common pond skater is about 1 centimetre long. They have six legs: the front ones are short and are used for holding prey. The middle pair of legs is very long and is used like oars, and the back pair is used for **steering**. The animals belong to the **true bugs** and have a piercing beak instead of jaws for chewing.

The surface of water behaves like a very thin, stretchy skin. This **surface tension** comes about because the water particles attract each other. On the pond skater's legs there are thousands of tiny hairs that are **water repellent**. So the legs only press small dents into the water without breaking through it. With powerful strokes of their middle legs they glide forward at lightning speed.

Pond skaters live on calm **fresh waters** such as ponds, small lakes, pools and slow flowing streams. There are several hundred species worldwide. A few species, the **sea skaters**, even live on the open ocean, far from land. Several species are found in Switzerland; the one seen most often is the common pond skater.

Pond skaters are **predators**. They mainly eat insects that have fallen into the water and are struggling, for example flies or midges. The movements of the prey create small ripples, which the pond skater feels with its legs. It grabs the animal with its front legs and sucks it out with its **piercing beak**.

Many pond skaters can fly and so find new waters when a pool dries up. The females lay their eggs on water plants. The adults usually spend the winter on land, hidden in leaves or moss on the bank. In spring they return to the water.

Scientists study pond skaters closely in order to learn from them. They have already built small **robots** that run across water like pond skaters or can even jump. Water repellent surfaces for clothing are also being developed on the model of animals and plants. This kind of research is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of water that makes it hold together at the surface like a thin skin.
A group of insects with a piercing beak with which they suck up food.
Made in such a way that water rolls off and does not soak in.
A science that develops inventions modelled on nature.

gewusst: If you put washing up liquid in the water, the surface tension becomes weaker and a pond skater would sink.
Some pond skaters live on the open sea, hundreds of kilometres from the coast.
Pond skaters notice prey that has fallen into the water by tiny ripples.

teile.einleitung: A hot water bottle is a soft container that you fill with hot water. It warms cold feet, heats the bed in advance or eases tummy ache. The fact that it stays warm for so long has to do with a special property of water.
wichtigste: A hot water bottle is filled with hot water.
Classic hot water bottles are made of rubber.
A fabric cover protects you from burning yourself.
After filling it, you must screw the stopper on tightly.
You should not fill it with boiling water, because the rubber can be damaged.
Overnight the water slowly cools down.
In Switzerland the cherry stone cushion is a popular alternative.

abschnitte.titel: What is a hot water bottle?
abschnitte.text: A **hot water bottle** is a flat bag with a screw stopper. You fill it with hot water and, for example, put it in your bed in the evening to warm it up. Many people also use it for cold feet, tummy ache or tense muscles. It is usually kept in a **cover** made of fabric or knitted wool. This makes sure you do not burn yourself on the hot surface.

Water can store a great deal of heat; it has a high **heat capacity**. To warm a litre of water by one degree takes more energy than for almost any other liquid. That is why a hot water bottle gives off its warmth slowly and evenly. Even so, the water slowly cools down overnight until it reaches the temperature of its surroundings. Under a duvet this happens more slowly, because the duvet holds the heat in.

Classic hot water bottles are made of **rubber** or soft plastic. Rubber is stretchy, watertight and does not conduct heat too quickly. In the past people used bed warmers made of metal, ceramic or glass. Even earlier, hot stones or pans of embers were put in the bed. Rubber hot water bottles have existed since the beginning of the 20th century.

You should not pour in boiling water, because the rubber can be damaged and there is a risk of scalding. Usually you fill the bottle only about two thirds full. Then you squeeze the air out and screw the **stopper** on tightly. This stops hot water from leaking out. Old, cracked hot water bottles should be replaced, because they can burst.

In Switzerland the **cherry stone cushion** is a popular alternative. It is a fabric bag full of dried cherry stones. You warm it up in the oven or the microwave. The stones store the heat and give it off slowly. Cooled in the freezer, the same cushion also helps with bumps and bruises.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much heat a substance can store when it gets warmer.
A stretchy, waterproof material, often made from the sap of the rubber tree.
An injury to the skin caused by hot water or steam.
A fabric cushion filled with cherry stones that you warm up or cool down.

gewusst: You can also fill a hot water bottle with cold water and use it as a cooling pad on hot summer days.
A kilogram of water stores several times as much heat as a kilogram of stones.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower is energy obtained from flowing or falling water. Centuries ago, waterwheels already drove mills; today, large power stations use it to produce electricity. In Switzerland, hydropower is the most important source of electricity.
wichtigste: Hydropower is the name for energy produced by flowing water.
In hydroelectric power stations, water drives a turbine that turns a generator.
Hydropower is renewable, because the water cycle is driven by the Sun.
There are run of river power stations, storage power stations and pumped storage power stations.
In Switzerland, about 60 per cent of electricity comes from hydropower (as of around 2024).
The Grande Dixence dam in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world.
But reservoirs and power stations also change rivers and habitats.

abschnitte.text: Water flowing downhill has energy of motion. Water in a high reservoir has **potential energy**, which is released when it falls down. This energy can be used to drive machines or to produce **electricity**. Because the Sun keeps evaporating water, which falls back as rain and snow, hydropower is a renewable energy.

abschnitte.titel: How does a power station work?
abschnitte.text: In the power station, water flows through a **turbine** and makes it turn. The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electricity. The higher the water falls from and the more water flows, the more electricity is produced. Well known types of turbine are the Pelton, the Francis and the Kaplan turbine.

**Run of river power stations** stand on rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare and use the constantly flowing water. **Storage power stations** collect water in reservoirs in the mountains and can supply electricity exactly when it is needed. Pumped storage power stations pump water upwards when there is spare electricity and let it flow down again later. They work like huge batteries.

Switzerland has many mountains, glaciers and lots of rain and snow, and is therefore also called the **water tower of Europe**. There are more than 600 larger hydroelectric power stations here. The Grande Dixence dam in Valais is 285 metres high, making it the highest gravity dam in the world. The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais, in operation since 2022, is one of the most powerful in Europe.

In ancient times, **waterwheels** already turned millstones for grinding grain. In the Middle Ages they drove saws, hammer mills and spinning mills, in many Swiss valleys too. Towards the end of the 19th century the first hydroelectric power stations for electricity were built. In the 20th century the big dams were built in the Alps, most of them between 1950 and 1970.

Hydropower supplies electricity with almost no **CO2** emissions and can be stored well. But reservoirs flood valleys, and power stations interrupt the natural course of rivers. Fish such as the lake trout can no longer migrate freely, so fish ladders are built. In addition, some streams below water intakes carry only a little water, which is why the law requires a **residual flow**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that is turned by the water.
A machine that makes electricity from rotation.
An artificial lake behind a dam that stores water.
Energy from sources that keep renewing themselves, such as water, sun or wind.
The water that must stay in the stream below a power station.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence dam weighs about 15 million tonnes, more than the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt.
A large part of the electricity for SBB trains comes from the railway's own hydroelectric power stations.
The largest hydroelectric power station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam in China.

teile.einleitung: Water vapour is water in the form of a gas. It forms when water boils or evaporates. Pure water vapour is actually invisible; the white clouds above a saucepan are tiny droplets of water.
wichtigste: Water vapour is water as a gas.
Real water vapour is invisible; visible clouds of steam are made of little droplets.
Warm vapour rises because it is lighter than the air.
Hot steam can scald the skin.
Steam pushes up the lid of a saucepan and makes a whistling kettle whistle.
With steam you can iron, clean, cook vegetables and froth up milk.
Steam engines changed the world in the 18th and 19th centuries.

abschnitte.text: When water is heated strongly, its particles move so fast that they break away from each other. **Water vapour** forms, an invisible gas. When the vapour cools in the air, tiny droplets form and we see white clouds of steam. This change from gas to liquid is called **condensation**, and this is also how clouds and fog form.

One litre of water makes more than a thousand litres of steam. That is why steam pushes up the lid of a saucepan, which then rattles. In a **whistling kettle**, the steam forces its way through a narrow opening and makes a whistling sound. Warm steam is lighter than the surrounding air and therefore rises.

Hot steam can **scald** the skin. When steam condenses on the skin, it also gives off a lot of heat, which is why it is often more dangerous than water at the same temperature. So always open a saucepan lid away from you. You should also not hold your hands or face over a kettle.

In the kitchen you can cook vegetables gently over steam, which keeps the vitamins in better. A steam iron uses hot steam to get creases out of clothes. A steam cleaner cleans floors and tiles without cleaning products. Coffee machines froth up milk with hot steam, and in a **sauna** hot steam forms when you pour water onto the hot stones.

In the 18th century the Scotsman James Watt greatly improved the **steam engine**. It powered factories, locomotives and ships and set off industrialisation. In Switzerland, historic paddle steamers still sail on lakes such as Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva today. The Brienz Rothorn Railway also climbs the mountain with steam locomotives.

The air always contains some water vapour; this is called **humidity**. Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. When moist air cools down, clouds, fog or dew form. Water vapour is also an important greenhouse gas that keeps the Earth warm.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change from gas to liquid, for example when steam turns into droplets.
A slow change from liquid to gas, even without boiling.
An injury to the skin caused by hot water or hot steam.
The amount of water vapour contained in the air.

gewusst: Right above the spout of a boiling kettle there is a small clear area; that is where the real, invisible steam is.
A bathroom mirror mists up because water vapour condenses on the cool glass.
The white trails behind aeroplanes are made of frozen water vapour from the engines.

teile.einleitung: Water pressure is the pressure that water exerts through its own weight on everything inside it. The deeper you dive, the harder the water presses. That is why dams, submarines and divers need special protection.
wichtigste: Water pressure comes from the weight of the water above a point.
For every 10 m of water depth, about 1 bar of pressure is added to the air pressure.
The pressure depends on the height of the water, not on the shape or size of the container.
Water presses equally hard from all sides, including from below and from the side.
Water pressure is greatest at the bottom of a lake.
In the salty sea the pressure is slightly higher than in a mountain lake, because salt water is heavier.
Water towers and reservoirs stand high up so that the water flows into houses with enough pressure.

abschnitte.text: Water has weight: one litre weighs about one kilogram. The more water lies above a point, the more heavily it presses on it. That is why **hydrostatic pressure** rises steadily with depth. At a depth of 10 m the water presses with about 100,000 newtons on every square metre, which is the weight of around 10 tonnes. Pressure is measured in **bar** or pascals.

If you make three holes one above the other in a plastic bottle and fill it with water, it squirts out most strongly and furthest from the lowest hole. That is where the column of water above it is highest. If you squeeze a filled water bag with a hole in it, the water squirts out harder, because the pressure spreads everywhere in the water. The **hydrostatic paradox** is surprising: at the same water height, the pressure on the bottom is the same, whether the container is wide or narrow.

Dams are much thicker at the bottom than at the top, because the pressure is greatest at the bottom of the reservoir. A **gravity dam** such as the Grande Dixence in Valais holds back the water by its enormous own weight. The water supply uses pressure too: reservoirs are often on a hill above the village. That way the water flows into the houses without any pump. On the ground floor it usually comes out of the tap with more pressure than on the top floor.

When diving, you feel the water pressure in your ears after only a few metres. Divers have to **equalise** the pressure so that their eardrums do not hurt. At a depth of 25 m, about 2.5 bar is added to the air pressure, making about 3.5 bar in total. Anyone surfacing from a great depth has to rise slowly so that the body can get used to the falling pressure.

At the deepest point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench, the pressure is more than 1000 bar. That is like a car standing on each of your fingernails. **Submarines** therefore have very thick, strong walls. The Swiss scientist **Auguste Piccard** developed the bathyscaphe Trieste, in which his son Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived almost 11 km down to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 1960. Deep sea fish survive there because their bodies contain hardly any air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water presses on a surface because of its weight.
A unit of pressure; air pressure at sea level is about 1 bar.
Pressure in still water, which increases with depth.
Balancing the pressure in your ears when diving.
A water store, often high up, for the drinking water supply.

gewusst: A diver at a depth of 10 m bears twice as much pressure as at the surface.
A polystyrene cup taken into the deep sea on a diving robot comes back up squashed tiny.
The Swiss Auguste Piccard first flew in a balloon into the stratosphere and then built submersibles for the deep sea.

teile.einleitung: A waterfall forms where a river or stream plunges over a rock edge into the depths. Gravity pulls the water downwards, often with a thundering roar and fine spray. Switzerland has many famous waterfalls, from the mighty Rhine Falls to the high falls of the Lauterbrunnen valley.
wichtigste: In a waterfall, water plunges downwards because of gravity.
The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen are the most famous large waterfall in Switzerland.
The Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland has particularly many waterfalls, for example the Staubbach Falls.
The Trümmelbach Falls near Lauterbrunnen thunder down inside a mountain.
The Giessbach Falls on Lake Brienz drop in 14 steps.
The highest waterfall in the world is Angel Falls in Venezuela.
The energy of falling water can be used in hydroelectric power stations.

abschnitte.text: Waterfalls form where a river flows over a **step in the land**. Often there is hard rock on top and softer rock below, which the water wears away faster. This creates an edge over which the water plunges. **Gravity** pulls the water down, making it go faster and faster. At the foot of the fall, the crashing water often digs out a deep basin called a **plunge pool**.

Many waterfalls in the Alps owe their existence to the **glaciers** of the Ice Ages. The glaciers scoured out wide, steep **U-shaped valleys**. The side streams could not cut down as deeply and today plunge over high rock walls into the main valley. The best known example is the Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland, where there are dozens of waterfalls. There, the Staubbach Falls drop almost 300 metres freely and turn into a fine dust of water.

The **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen are about 150 metres wide and about 23 metres high. They are considered one of the waterfalls with the most water in Europe. The **Trümmelbach Falls** near Lauterbrunnen are special because they thunder down inside the mountain, carrying meltwater from the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau. On Lake Brienz, the **Giessbach Falls** plunge down to the lake in 14 steps. There are many others too, such as the Reichenbach Falls near Meiringen.

The highest waterfall in the world is **Angel Falls** in Venezuela, whose water falls almost 1000 metres. Niagara Falls on the border between Canada and the USA are famous for their huge amounts of water. The Iguazú Falls between Argentina and Brazil are made up of hundreds of separate falls. The local people call the Victoria Falls in Africa “the smoke that thunders”. They lie on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Falling water has a lot of **energy**, which on impact is turned into movement, noise and a little heat. This energy is used in **hydroelectric power stations**, where water falls through pipes onto turbines. In Switzerland, most electricity comes from hydropower. Fine spray often forms at waterfalls, and in sunshine a **rainbow** appears in it. Because the rocks are wet and slippery, you should always stay on the paths at waterfalls.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the Earth pulls all things downwards.
A deep basin at the foot of a waterfall that the water has hollowed out.
A wide valley with steep sides that a glacier has scoured out.
A plant that produces electricity from the energy of flowing or falling water.

gewusst: Waterfalls slowly move backwards, because the water wears away the rock edge bit by bit.
At the Rhine Falls you can take a boat to a rock in the middle of the roaring water.
In winter, smaller waterfalls can freeze solid and are then climbed by ice climbers.

teile.einleitung: Heat transfer is the name for all the processes by which heat gets from one place to another. There are three kinds: conduction, convection and radiation. Whether cooking, heating or sunbathing, heat transfer is always involved.
wichtigste: Heat is transferred in three ways: by conduction, convection and radiation.
On its own, heat always flows from the warmer to the colder.
Conduction needs contact between particles.
In convection, a flowing liquid or gas carries the heat.
Thermal radiation also works through a vacuum.
The Sun's warmth reaches us by radiation.
A vacuum flask slows down all three kinds of heat transfer.

abschnitte.text: When two things are at different temperatures, heat flows from the warmer to the colder. This goes on until both are equally warm. This balancing out is called **heat transfer**. Depending on the situation it happens by conduction, convection or radiation, and often by all three at once.

In **conduction**, particles pass their movement on to their neighbours without the substance itself moving. This needs contact, that is, a material through which the heat travels. If you put a metal spoon in hot tea, the handle soon gets warm too. Metals conduct heat well; air, wood and plastic conduct it poorly.

In **convection**, the warm substance itself moves. Warm air is lighter than cold air and therefore rises; this is how a radiator spreads heat round a room. In a saucepan, warm water rises from the bottom and colder water sinks. Wind and ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream also carry huge amounts of heat.

Every warm body gives off invisible **infrared radiation**. This **thermal radiation** needs no material and even travels through the vacuum of space. That is how the Sun's warmth reaches the Earth across about 150 million kilometres. At a campfire you feel it on your face, even when the air around you is cool.

The most important difference: conduction needs contact, radiation also works through a vacuum. That is why a cup of tea on a table can conduct heat into the table, but in space it can cool down only by radiation. Light coloured and shiny surfaces reflect thermal radiation, dark surfaces absorb it. Survival blankets therefore have a shiny silver side.

A **vacuum flask** has two walls of glass or steel with a vacuum between them. The vacuum prevents conduction and convection, and the mirrored walls reflect the radiation. This keeps tea hot or juice cold for hours. The Scottish scientist James Dewar invented this principle in 1892.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heat travels through a material from particle to particle.
Heat is carried along by a flowing liquid or gas.
Invisible radiation that carries heat even through empty space.
A space that is almost completely empty, with no air.

gewusst: Without thermal radiation, no warmth from the Sun would reach us, because the space in between is almost empty.
With thermal imaging cameras you can see the thermal radiation of people and animals even in the dark.
A hairdryer warms your hair mainly by convection: it blows warm air onto it.

teile.einleitung: A heat pump is a device that takes heat from the surroundings and releases it inside the house. It draws the heat from the air, the ground or groundwater and needs only a little electricity to do so. In Switzerland, heat pumps are very often fitted in new houses today.
wichtigste: A heat pump takes heat from the surroundings and releases it in the house.
It works like a fridge in reverse.
The heat source can be outdoor air, the ground or groundwater.
A refrigerant absorbs heat, is compressed and gives off the heat again at a higher temperature.
From one unit of electricity it makes about three to five units of heat.
Heat pumps do not burn oil or gas and are therefore climate friendly.
Many heat pumps can also cool in summer.

abschnitte.text: A heat pump is a **heating system** that does not produce heat itself but pumps it into the house from outside. Even cold winter air still contains heat energy that can be used. The heat pump raises this heat to a higher temperature that is enough for heating and hot water. To do this it needs electricity for a **compressor**.

Inside the heat pump, a **refrigerant** flows round a closed circuit. It evaporates even at very low temperatures and in doing so absorbs heat from the surroundings. The compressor squeezes the vapour, which makes it very hot, just as a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump up a tyre. In the house the hot refrigerant gives its heat to the heating water, cools down, is allowed to expand, and the cycle starts again.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the heat come from?
abschnitte.text: An **air source heat pump** takes heat from the outdoor air; you can recognise it by the fan outside the house. A **ground source heat pump** uses heat from the ground; for this, holes more than 100 metres deep are often drilled. Deep down it is roughly the same temperature all year round. Other systems use groundwater, lake water or waste heat.

A **fridge** is actually a heat pump too. It pumps heat out of the inside and releases it at the back into the kitchen, which is why it is warm there. The heat pump in a heating system does the same, only it brings heat from outside to inside. Some systems can switch over and cool the house in summer.

From one kilowatt hour of electricity, a good heat pump makes about three to five kilowatt hours of heat. This figure is called the **seasonal performance factor**. Ground source heat pumps are usually more efficient than air source heat pumps, because the ground is warmer than the air in winter. Heat pumps work best with underfloor heating, which needs only moderately warm water.

In Switzerland, heat pumps are now fitted in most new detached houses. Many old oil and gas heating systems are also being replaced by heat pumps, often with grants from the cantons. Because Swiss electricity comes mostly from hydropower and nuclear energy, heat pumps cause little **CO2**. They are therefore seen as an important technology for protecting the climate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that evaporates even at low temperatures and carries heat.
A pump that squeezes a gas together and so heats it up.
A pipe deep in the ground through which liquid flows and picks up heat from the earth.
Shows how much heat a heat pump delivers per unit of electricity over a year.

gewusst: Even at minus 10 °C outside, an air source heat pump can still take heat from the air.
As early as the 19th century, Lord Kelvin described the idea of a heat pump.
From 1938, Zurich's town hall was heated by one of the first large heat pumps in Europe, which took heat from the River Limmat.

teile.einleitung: Hydrogen is the lightest element and could become an important energy carrier of the future. It can be made from water using electricity, stored, and later turned back into electricity or heat. The only exhaust is water, but a lot of energy is lost along the way.
wichtigste: Hydrogen is the lightest element in the periodic table.
In electrolysis, water is split into hydrogen and oxygen with the help of electricity.
A fuel cell produces electricity directly from hydrogen and oxygen.
Green hydrogen is made with electricity from renewable energy.
Most hydrogen today is grey hydrogen made from natural gas.
In fuel cell cars, hydrogen is usually stored at about 700 bar.
Making hydrogen and turning it back into electricity loses much more energy than a battery does.

abschnitte.text: **Hydrogen** has the chemical symbol H and comes right at the start of the periodic table. A hydrogen atom consists of just one proton and one electron. Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe; the Sun is made mostly of it. On Earth it is found almost only in compounds, for example in water. As a gas it is colourless, odourless and very easily set alight.

Hydrogen is not an energy source like the sun or wind but an **energy carrier**. You first have to put energy in to make it. In **electrolysis**, electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen can be stored and transported. Later it gives the energy back, for example in a fuel cell.

Depending on how it is made, hydrogen is given a colour. **Green hydrogen** is made with electricity from the sun, wind or hydropower and is climate friendly. **Grey hydrogen** comes from natural gas, and a lot of carbon dioxide is produced in the process. It makes up most of the production today. With blue hydrogen, the carbon dioxide is captured and stored.

A **fuel cell** lets hydrogen and oxygen react with each other in a controlled way and produces electricity directly. Only water vapour comes out of the exhaust. In the tanks of fuel cell cars, hydrogen is usually stored at about 700 bar, which is about 300 times more pressure than in a bicycle tyre. In Switzerland, lorries running on hydrogen have been on the roads since 2020. Hydrogen is also being tested for trains, ships and industry.

Hydrogen can store energy from the summer and make it usable in winter. A big **disadvantage** is that a lot of energy is lost in making, storing and turning it back into electricity. In the end often only about a third is left, whereas with a battery it is much more. In addition, hydrogen and oxygen form the explosive **oxyhydrogen**. That is why tight tanks, sensors and strict safety rules are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that stores and transports energy, for example petrol or hydrogen.
A process in which electricity breaks a substance such as water down into its parts.
A device that produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.
An explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.
A unit of pressure; the air around us is at about 1 bar.

gewusst: A kilogram of hydrogen contains about three times as much energy as a kilogram of petrol.
The airship Hindenburg was filled with hydrogen and went up in flames in 1937.

teile.einleitung: When you sit in front of a campfire, you feel the heat on your face, even though the hot air rises upwards. This is due to thermal radiation. It is invisible light that every body gives off, and it even brings the Sun's warmth to us through empty space.
wichtigste: All bodies give off thermal radiation, depending on their temperature.
Thermal radiation is mostly infrared radiation, which our eyes cannot see.
William Herschel discovered infrared radiation in the year 1800.
Thermal radiation does not need air and even travels through the vacuum of space.
A black body absorbs all the radiation that falls on it completely.
If the absolute temperature doubles, the power radiated rises sixteenfold.
Shiny surfaces such as a survival blanket reflect thermal radiation.

abschnitte.text: **Thermal radiation** is a form of electromagnetic radiation, just like light and radio waves. Every body gives it off, an ice cube just as much as the Sun. At room temperature it lies in the range of **infrared radiation**, which we cannot see but can feel on our skin. Very hot bodies such as red hot iron or the filament of an old light bulb also glow visibly red, yellow or white. Heat can also spread by conduction and by convection, but radiation is the only way that needs no material at all.

In the year 1800 the astronomer **William Herschel** split sunlight into its colours with a prism. He placed thermometers in the different colours. Next to the red light, where nothing could be seen at all, the temperature rose the most. In this way he discovered invisible **infrared radiation**. Herschel was born in Germany and lived in England, where he also found the planet Uranus.

An ideal **black body** absorbs all the radiation that hits it and is itself a particularly good radiator. Dark, matt surfaces come close to this, whereas shiny surfaces reflect radiation. The power radiated grows with the fourth power of the absolute temperature; this is described by the **Stefan-Boltzmann law**. So if you double the temperature in kelvin, the radiation rises by a factor of 16. That is why a fire radiates so much more strongly than a warm stove.

Under a **sunshade** it is more pleasant, even though the air is almost the same temperature, because it blocks the Sun's radiation. A car in the sun gets very hot inside: light comes in through the windows, but the thermal radiation from the hot seats hardly gets out. The Earth's greenhouse effect works in a similar way. A silver **survival blanket** reflects the body's thermal radiation and keeps injured people warm. A vacuum flask is also mirrored on the inside.

With a **thermal imaging camera** you can make thermal radiation visible. Warm spots appear bright or red, cold ones dark or blue. Fire brigades use this to find people in smoke filled rooms or hidden pockets of embers. On a house, the camera shows where heat escapes through poor insulation. Some snakes, such as pit vipers, sense the thermal radiation of their prey with special sense organs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible radiation beyond red that you feel as heat.
An imaginary body that absorbs all radiation and is a particularly good radiator.
Temperature in kelvin, counted from absolute zero at about minus 273 °C.
A camera that makes thermal radiation visible as a picture.

gewusst: You yourself are constantly giving off heat; in a thermal imaging camera you glow brightly.
All the energy that reaches the Earth from the Sun comes as radiation through empty space.

teile.einleitung: A watermill uses the force of flowing water to drive machines. For centuries such mills ground grain into flour, sawed wood or forged iron. They are the ancestors of today's hydroelectric power stations.
wichtigste: A watermill is driven by a waterwheel.
If the water falls onto the wheel from above, it is called overshot.
A channel, the mill race, leads the water to the millwheel.
Through gearwheels, the waterwheel turns the millstone.
In sawmills tree trunks were sawn up, and in hammer mills iron was forged.
Old waterwheels were mostly built of wood.
Today's hydroelectric power stations use a turbine instead of a millwheel.

abschnitte.text: A **mill race** leads water from a river or stream to the millwheel. The water presses on the paddles or fills small buckets, and the wheel starts to turn. Through a shaft and **gearwheels**, the rotation is carried into the inside of the mill. There the heavy upper **millstone** turns above a fixed lower stone. The grain is ground into flour between them.

With an **overshot** wheel, the water falls into the buckets from above, and the weight of the water turns the wheel. It suits small streams with a steep drop, as are often found in hills and mountains. With an **undershot** wheel, the water flows against the paddles at the bottom, which suits wide, flat rivers. In between there is the breastshot wheel. Old waterwheels were mostly built of wood and often had to be repaired.

Water power did not drive only grain mills. In the **sawmill**, in Switzerland often called a “Sagi”, tree trunks were sawn into planks. In the **hammer mill**, the waterwheel lifted a heavy hammer that struck red hot iron. Other mills pressed oil, pounded rags into paper or drove looms. That is why whole villages and trades grew up along streams and rivers.

The Greeks and **Romans** already knew about watermills. At Barbegal in southern France, the Romans ran a site with 16 waterwheels. In the Middle Ages watermills spread across the whole of Europe, and almost every village had one. The miller was an important man, because everyone needed flour for their bread. With the steam engine and later the electric motor, many mills lost their job.

Today's **hydroelectric power stations** use a **turbine** instead of a millwheel. It turns much faster and drives a generator that produces electricity. In Switzerland, more than half of the electricity comes from hydropower. Many old mills are museums today or have been converted into small power stations. In some you can still watch the wheel turning and flour being ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: A channel that leads water to the millwheel.
A heavy, round stone used to grind grain into flour.
A waterwheel onto which the water falls from above.
A fast turning bladed wheel in modern power stations.

gewusst: The common surname Müller (Miller in English) is a reminder of how many people used to work in mills.
A big waterwheel often turned only a few times a minute, but it had a lot of power.

teile.einleitung: The water pistol is a popular toy for hot summer days. Press the trigger and a jet of water shoots out. Behind it lies exciting physics about pressure, pumps and the path of water through the air.
wichtigste: In a simple water pistol, a small pump pushes water out.
The faster and harder you press, the stronger the jet.
With big water pistols, you first pump air together in the tank.
The squeezed air pushes the water out; over time the jet gets weaker.
A jet of water always falls downwards in a curve.
The jet flies furthest when you aim at a slant upwards.
You should never aim at other people's eyes.

abschnitte.text: A simple **water pistol** has a tank, a trigger and a small **pump**. When you pull the trigger, a piston pushes water out through a narrow nozzle. Small **valves** make sure the water flows in one direction only. When you let go, the pump sucks new water in from the tank. The faster and harder you press, the stronger the jet.

With big water pistols, you pump several times before squirting. This squeezes the **air in the tank**, and the pressure rises. When you open the valve, the air pushes the water out powerfully. The more water flows out, the more room the air has, and the pressure falls. That is why the jet gets weaker if you squirt for a long time, and if the tank has a hole, the air escapes and the jet stays weak.

If you squirt straight ahead, the jet of water falls downwards in a **curve**. Gravity pulls the water down while it flies forwards. This path is called a **parabola**. Without air resistance, the jet flies furthest if you aim upwards at an angle of 45 degrees. Fountains and garden hoses show such curves too.

The famous water pistol **Super Soaker** was invented by the American engineer **Lonnie Johnson**. He worked for the space agency NASA and was experimenting with a pump in the 1980s. A powerful jet of water shot across his bathroom. From 1990 the Super Soaker was sold and became one of the most successful toys in the world. It uses exactly the principle of squeezed air.

With a water pistol you should never aim at other people's **eyes**, because a strong jet can injure the eyes. You also do not squirt at animals, electrical appliances or people who do not want to play. It is best to fill it with clean water. After playing, you empty the tank so that no germs grow. In summer, a water fight is a welcome way to cool down.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow opening through which water shoots out fast.
A small flap that lets water or air through in one direction only.
How hard something presses on a surface, for example air in the tank.
The curved path of something that is thrown or squirted.

gewusst: The inventor of the Super Soaker has registered more than a hundred patents.
As it flies, a jet of water breaks up into many small drops, which you can see well against the light.

teile.einleitung: A hydroelectric power station produces electricity from the force of flowing or falling water. In Switzerland, hydropower is the most important source of electricity, thanks to the many mountains, lakes and rivers. The water drives a turbine, and a generator turns this into electricity.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, most electricity comes from hydropower; in 2024 it was about 60 per cent.
A hydroelectric power station uses the potential and kinetic energy of water.
Water drives a turbine, which produces electricity with a generator.
There are river power stations, storage power stations with reservoirs and pumped storage power stations.
Hydropower is renewable, because it keeps raining and snowing.
Hydroelectric power stations produce hardly any CO2 and no smoke.
Fish ladders help fish to swim past river power stations.

abschnitte.text: Water that lies high up has **potential energy**. When it flows or falls down, this becomes **kinetic energy**. The water flows through a **turbine** and turns it like a windmill. The turbine is connected to a generator, which turns the rotation into electric current. The more water flows and the further it falls, the more electricity is produced.

A **river power station** stands on a river and uses a lot of water with a small drop, for example on the Rhine and the Aare. A **storage power station** collects water in a reservoir high in the mountains and, when needed, lets it plunge far down through pipes. A pumped storage power station pumps water into a higher lake when there is plenty of spare electricity. When a lot of electricity is needed later, it lets the water flow down again. In this way it works like a giant battery.

For big drops in the Alps, the **Pelton turbine** is used. In it, a sharp jet of water shoots onto spoon shaped buckets on a wheel. For small drops and lots of water, as in river power stations, the **Kaplan turbine** is suitable; it looks like a ship's propeller. In between, the Francis turbine is often used. The Pelton turbine was invented in the USA in the 19th century.

Switzerland is sometimes called the water tower of Europe, because many big rivers rise here. In Valais and the Grisons there are numerous reservoirs, such as the Lac des Dix behind the **Grande Dixence** dam. The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais went into operation in 2022 and lies deep inside the mountain. On the Rhine at Rheinfelden stands one of the oldest large river power stations in Europe. In winter, the storage lakes supply particularly valuable electricity, when other sources supply less.

Hydroelectric power stations produce hardly any CO2 and are therefore good for the climate. They can supply electricity very quickly when it is needed. But dams greatly change valleys and rivers, and fish can no longer migrate freely. That is why **fish ladders** are built and care is taken that enough **residual flow** stays in the streams. In the past, people used waterwheels to grind corn in mills or to drive saws.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that turns because of flowing water.
A machine that turns rotation into electricity.
An artificial lake behind a dam that stores water.
A power station that pumps water up and later lets it down again to produce electricity.
Water that must stay in the stream below a power station so that animals and plants can live.

gewusst: The largest hydroelectric power station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze in China.
A pumped storage power station uses more electricity for pumping than it produces later, but it is still useful as a store.
The Romans already used waterwheels to grind grain.

teile.einleitung: Water is the most important substance for all life on Earth. Pure water is transparent and has no smell and no taste. It can occur as a solid in the form of ice, as a liquid, or as a gas in the form of water vapour.
wichtigste: Pure water is transparent, odourless and tasteless.
At 20 degrees Celsius water is liquid; at 0 °C it freezes and at 100 °C it boils.
Liquid water takes the shape of any container you pour it into.
Our body is made up of slightly more than half water.
Schoolchildren should drink about one litre a day.
The chemical formula of water is H2O.
Switzerland is known as the water tower of Europe.

abschnitte.text: Water is made of tiny **molecules**, each built from two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. That is why its chemical formula is **H2O**. In a glass, pure water is transparent, but in a deep lake or in the sea it has a bluish shimmer. Water is measured in litres, for example in a measuring jug.

At 20 degrees Celsius water is liquid and takes the shape of any bowl you pour it into. At 0 °C it freezes into **ice**, and at 100 °C it starts to boil at sea level. On high mountains water boils at less than 100 °C, because the air pressure is lower. What is special is that ice is lighter than liquid water and therefore floats on top.

Our body is made up of slightly more than half water, and babies have even more. We constantly lose water through sweating, breathing and going to the toilet. That is why schoolchildren should drink about one litre a day, ideally water or unsweetened tea. In hot weather and during sport you need even more.

About 70 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered with water. Most of it is salty seawater; only a few per cent is **fresh water**. Water is constantly on the move in the **water cycle**: it evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and flows back to the sea through rivers. A sponge put in water soaks it up, because water creeps into fine hollow spaces.

Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**, because big rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhone, the Inn and the Ticino rise here. Glaciers, lakes and groundwater store huge amounts of water. Drinking water comes mostly from groundwater and springs and is usually so clean that you can drink it straight from the tap. But if a fountain says “Kein Trinkwasser” (not drinking water), you should not drink from it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest particle of a substance; for water it is made of three atoms.
Water with very little salt, as in lakes, rivers and groundwater.
The constant journey of water between the sea, the air, the land and rivers.
Water that collects underground in soil and rock.

gewusst: Water is one of the few substances that is lighter as a solid than as a liquid, which is why lakes freeze from the top.
The water you drink today may once have been inside a dinosaur or in a cloud over the Pacific.
On a tap, the red side usually means warm water and the blue side cold water.
